newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea wants to bring N.Korean defector to Seoul.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea wants to bring N.Korean defector to Seoul.

text.p: South Korea is to seek to bring a senior North Korean defector directly to Seoul from China when it resumes talks on his fate after the funeral of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, Seoul officials said on Monday.
Talks on the fate of North Korea's top ideologue, Hwang Jang-yop, were put on hold after Deng's death last Wednesday, with all contacts reduced to working level, they said.

"We will meet Chinese officials on February 26 and convey our basic stand that Hwang's free will to come to South Korea must be respected," Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung told Reuters. Deng's funeral is set for Tuesday.

"We would like to bring Hwang directly to Seoul but technical details will be worked out through consultations with China," Lee said. "If the direct route is not possible, we would discuss other options."

Hwang, ranked 24th in the Pyongyang hierarchy, has been marooned at Seoul's consular office in Beijing since February 12 when he turned up there with an aide to seek asylum. This left China torn between long-time ideological ally North Korea and new business partner South Korea.
Lee denied media reports that China and South Korea had already reached basic agreement for Hwang to leave Beijing before the end of this week.
"We have had no substantive contacts with the Chinese officials since Deng Xiaoping's death and we have not reached any agreement," he said.

Pyongyang initially accused Southern officials of kidnapping Hwang and demanded that China return him to the North but later appeared to backtrack, saying that if it transpired that he had defected he would be stripped of his official rank.

China's official Xinhua news agency finally indicated last week that Beijing had determined that Hwang entered the South Korean mission of his own free will. A Seoul official said this suggested that talks over Hwang could now make rapid progress.
Information Minister Oh In-hwan was asked in parliament if Seoul's announcement of Hwang's defection had angered China and caused a delay in Hwang's departure.
Oh said: "I understand the talks on Hwang Jang-yon's defection are proceeding without major hurdles." .
But another government official said the talks on Hwang could still be affected by current uncertainty in North Korea, which has now lost three senior figures in less than two weeks.
Within 10 days of Hwang's defection, Pyongyang revealed that ailing premier Kang Song-san had stepped down and then announced the death of powerful defence minister Choe Kwang from a heart attack.

Seoul's deputy National Unification minister, Lee Ho, told Reuters he still expected North Korean leader Kim Jong-il formally to take over the key posts of state president and general secretary of the ruling party after the third anniversary in July of the death of his father Kim Il-sung, Pyongyang's founding leader.
"I think North Korea will announce a major leadership reshuffle shortly before or after Kim Jong-il's formal accession," Lee said.
Yu Suk-ryul, senior fellow at Seoul's state-backed Institute of Foreign Affairs and National Security, said the North now appeared unlikely to be able to stop Hwang from leaving China.
"North Korea appears to be seeking help from the West by sending out conciliatory signals," he said.

Pyongyang announced last Friday that it would attend a preliminary briefing in New York on March 5 on Korean Peninsula peace talks proposed by the United States and South Korea, which would also include China.

The concession followed promises by Washington and Seoul to send $10 million and $6 million respectively in food aid to the failing Stalinist state, which remains technically at war with South Korea nearly half a century after their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.
